For those of you just tuning in, Welcome to Prompt of the Day, a subverse based around generating new creative writings via picture prompts. If you're an aspiring or seasoned writer, check us out. We're quite friendly and will help you out!

Hello, and welcome to a new segment called "The Writer's Block," where we discuss our problems in continuing stories and creating new ones. I'm gr33narrow, and I'll be your host.

So we had an awesome recent boom in content this week. While it's fantastic, I also think most of our brains are a little fuzzy. I know I'm going through a writer's block now! After nearly a month of non stop writing, editing, and reviewing, I feel like I need to go watch cartoons and eat cereal in my batman onesie pajamas -- in a blanket fort.

Some of the rest of you also told me that your brains are pooped. So I figured "Hey, let's share ways we try to get back into the groove of things." Mostly so we don't feel like kids coming back to school from winter vacation.

So, tell me, what are your ways of getting over the dreaded block? What would be a fun break to ease us back into the flow we were in without overwhelming us? What are some of the issues that plague you -- is it a certain story (or 3, in my case) that's got you bogged down? Why does it bog you down?

All that and more on this Weekend's Issue of "THE WRITER'S BLOCK."
The Writer's Block --- New Discussion. Go ahead and list your qualms here!

The immense skill gap that lies between our prosaic little word-doodles and published works is staggeringly intimidating. When will I ever find the time -- or more pertinently, the strength of character -- to buckle down and learn every single goddamn thing there is to learn about writing? Impossible. Worlduilding takes a ridiculous amount of time to do properly, character creation requires ways of making individuals interesting and worthy of the fantasy they partake in, and plot is just fantastically insane to get a novitiate's grasp over.

How much time before one gets to a state in which they can look back at their works with satisfaction that lingers? Achieving a pride in wordsmithing that allows one to boast of their exploits and live up to the idiotic exaggerations you spout to your friends -- who, in interest of keeping your company, pretend to enjoy what you've written, perhaps submit a half-hearted critique if they're the slightest bit motivated -- is like trying to throw tennis balls at the stars. You may get meters higher, but these are insignificant improvements.

For those of us who have put years and hours of work into potential garbage -- when will we be satisfied? Unless one gets published (farther than the stars -- trying to hit the edge of the universe with your severed hand, more like) or achieves some renown, there is absolutely no reward to writing. Sure, you can write for yourself, but where's the fun in that? I want the reader to explore the illusion I've constructed for them, enlighten them or give them some joyful repose from a life that's a hundred times worse than that of my manufactured problems. I want to be relevant. I want to tell tales and adventures. I want people to care.

And that's the fucking joke, isn't it? The best writers write because they must write. Me, with my piddlingly inefficient toolkit, must aspire towards that goal with a mockery of true writing. I don't write because I want people to have fun. I write because I'm an egotistical little creature wasting away in insignificance, compensating for my inability to have a measurable impact on anything useful with reams of garbage: theme-less drivel that leaves the reader no better off than before. They only read me because they're unaware of or too lazy to read truly great works.

Can one change one's motivation? I'm not sure. I hope so.

Better than drugs, better 16 hour game marathons. Neutral, not negative. What fun.

Time to patch up my resolve and pretend like I'm improving. Maybe write something. Who knows.
